extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in geometric analysis and Ricci flow (mathematicians)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and justify the structural/quantitative assumptions used to construct long-time solutions to the Ricci flow with surgery (canonical neighborhood assumption, noncollapsing, δ-cutoff surgeries, parameter sequences, and related estimates). Applies to surgically modified solutions on compact orientable three-manifolds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical neighborhood assumption (accuracy ε)
rubrics_metrics.description: The solution (possibly surgically modified) satisfies the canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy ε on a time interval with an associated positive function r(t): at high curvature scales points have neighborhoods that are either strong ε-necks or ε-caps with specified gradient and curvature control (as in Theorem 7.1.1 / Lemma 7.3.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a central structural hypothesis for inductive construction of long-time flows with surgery. The text emphasizes the need to obtain this assumption uniformly (a single nonincreasing r(t) independent of the induction step k). One may invoke Theorem 7.1.1 to get canonical neighborhoods for smooth solutions and adapt Lemma 7.3.5 and Lemma 7.3.6 to surgically modified solutions. Violations of this assumption at a chosen earliest time are used to derive contradictions via rescaling arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: κ-noncollapsed on scales less than ρ (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A surgically modified solution gij(t) is κ-noncollapsed at (x0,t0) on scales less than ρ if: whenever r<ρ and |Rm(x,t)| ≤ r^{-2} for all (x,t) in P(x0,t0,r,-r^2) where the solution is defined, then Vol_{t0}(B_{t0}(x0,r)) ≥ κ r^3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This quantitative noncollapsing condition is crucial to apply compactness (Hamilton) and reduced volume arguments. Lemma 7.4.2 establishes existence of a κ>0 under the proposition's hypotheses (after choosing δ small depending on r and ε and previously constructed sequences). The proof localizes Perelman's reduced-volume argument to the surgery-unaffected region and estimates reduced length of barely admissible curves to handle surgeries.

rubrics_metrics.name: δ(t)-cutoff surgery requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Each surgery at time t in the surgically modified solution on (0,T) is a δ(t)-cutoff surgery (δ(t) small). Proposition 7.4.1 requires a prescribed decreasing sequence of δ_j and defines δ(t)=δ_j on time intervals [(j-1)ε^2, jε^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposition demands δ_j be sufficiently small (e.g., δ_j < ε^2 and other smallness conditions) and decreasing, and that δ(t) also satisfy δ(t) ≤ min{δ(t), ¯δ(t)} at surgery times. Choosing δ_j small enough serves two purposes: (1) push surgical regions to spatial infinity after rescaling (Perelman's idea) and (2) preserve the ability to apply local compactness and Shi-type derivative estimates on uniform small time intervals. Concrete smallness thresholds (e.g., depending on L,r,m,ε in intermediate claims) are given in proofs (existence of ¯δ(L,r,rm,ε) etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalized initial metric and compact orientability
rubrics_metrics.description: The surgically modified flow must start on a compact orientable three-manifold with normalized initial metric (normalization as in the text; scalar curvature control at initial time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the baseline geometric setting for the global surgery construction. Normalization (e.g., scalar curvature ≥ -1 everywhere after normalization) is used in maximum principle arguments and base-time reduced-volume estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite number of surgeries on finite time intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: For the proposition's setup, the flow has only a finite number of surgeries in the considered time interval (0,T).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finite surgeries assumption simplifies localization arguments; Proposition 7.4.1 is stated for flows with finite surgeries on [0,T). The inductive construction then shows one can extend solutions step-by-step; preventing accumulation of surgery times is a main difficulty addressed by uniform choices of parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pinching assumption preserved under surgery
rubrics_metrics.description: The extended surgically modified solution still satisfies the (Hamilton) pinching assumption (with accuracy ε) on the extended time interval after surgery (cf. Lemma 7.3.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to guarantee nonnegativity-type curvature control and to deduce, when combined with other estimates, that certain high-curvature regions must be modeled on standard solutions (necks/caps). This underpins canonical neighborhood descriptions and some curvature comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of uniform nonincreasing scale function r(t)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a single nonincreasing positive function r(t), defined on [0,∞), independent of induction index k, such that each ri(t) chosen in successive steps satisfies ri(t) ≥ r(t) on their domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniformity of r(t) across surgery steps is the key to prevent accumulation of surgery times and to justify the canonical neighborhood assumption for the indefinitely extending solution. Achieved by restricting ¯δ(t) and constructing decreasing sequences r_j appropriately in Proposition 7.4.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of decreasing sequences δ_j, r_j, κ_j with interval assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Given ε>0, there exist decreasing sequences 0<δ_1>δ_2>... , r_j<ε, κ_j>0 and the piecewise-constant function δ(t) with δ(t)=δ_j on t∈[(j-1)ε^2,jε^2) such that on each such time interval the surgically modified solution satisfies κ_j-noncollapsing on scales < ε and the canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy ε and scale r_j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the main statement of Proposition 7.4.1. It prescribes how surgery and scale parameters are coordinated in time-slab blocks of size ε^2 so that local geometric control (noncollapsing + canonical neighborhoods) holds uniformly on each block. The proof proceeds by induction on m (number of blocks) using Lemma 7.4.2 to produce κ and adapting canonical neighborhood and compactness arguments to surgical solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible vs barely admissible space-time curves
rubrics_metrics.description: A space-time curve is admissible if it stays in the surgery-unaffected region; it is barely admissible if it lies on the boundary of admissible curves (i.e., first to touch surgery regions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction is used to localize Perelman's reduced-length/reduced-volume arguments in the presence of surgeries. A key technical claim (7.4.2 and following) produces lower bounds on the L-length (or L+) of any barely admissible curve provided δ is chosen sufficiently small; this ensures minimizing L-geodesics avoid surgery regions and compactness/monotonicity arguments remain valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower bounds on L+-length of barely admissible curves (estimate 7.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any prescribed L<∞ and r<ε, there exists ¯δ(L,r,rm,ε)>0 such that every barely admissible curve γ from (x0,t0) to surgery-glued caps satisfies ∫_{T0}^{t0} sqrt(t0-t)(R+ + |γ̇|^2) dt ≥ L (estimate (7.4.2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This quantitative control prevents short reduced-length connections that pass through surgery regions; it is a technical tool to guarantee reduced-volume minimizers are realized by admissible curves and enables lower bounds on reduced volume near chosen points. The proof combines curvature control, Cauchy-Schwarz, and Corollary 7.3.7 type estimates; ¯δ depends on L,r,m,ε.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower bound for Perelman's reduced volume via cone-like sets and Jacobian comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: If one finds a point (x̄,t̄) on a minimizing L-geodesic with small earlier time slice and a ball of radius ~r_m contained in surgery-unaffected region, then Perelman's reduced volume of that ball at a slightly earlier time is bounded below by a positive constant depending only on κ_m and r_m, using the cone-like subset of shortest L-geodesics and Perelman's Jacobian comparison (Theorem 3.2.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This chain of estimates (reduced-length lower bounds, canonical neighborhood gradient bounds, admissibility of geodesics, and Jacobian comparison) yields the volume lower bound needed in Lemma 7.4.2. It is a localized version of Perelman's monotonicity adapted to surgical flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pushing surgical regions to infinity via choosing δ small
rubrics_metrics.description: When performing rescaling limits to analyze potential violations of the canonical neighborhood assumption, one chooses δ_{m+1} sufficiently small so that surgical regions are pushed arbitrarily far away in space after rescaling (Perelman's idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enables extraction of a limit (via Hamilton compactness) of the rescaled solutions which is smooth on compact sets; combined with κ-noncollapsing and Shi derivative estimates on small uniform time intervals, one can obtain an ancient κ-solution limit and reach a contradiction if canonical neighborhoods were violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local curvature and gradient control in canonical neighborhoods (estimates like 7.3.4 and standard solution bounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within canonical neighborhoods (ε-necks, ε-caps, standard solution regions) one has uniform curvature and derivative (gradient) estimates; e.g., bounds of the form |Rm| ≤ C R(·) on specified parabolic neighborhoods and explicit standard-solution curvature decay bounds (Proposition 7.3.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These estimates permit time-extension arguments (Steps 1–3), control of rescaled neighborhoods, and application of Shi's estimates to get higher-derivative bounds. They also allow comparison of scalar curvature values in nearby points (multiplicative comparison constants) and are used in Assertions 1–3 to preclude surgeries interfering with selected parabolic neighborhoods when parameters are chosen appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescaling and extraction of ancient κ-solution limits for contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: If canonical neighborhood assumption is violated at earliest time ¯t at some (¯x,¯t), rescale the solution around (¯x,¯t) by factor R(¯x,¯t) and shift time to zero; if δ and other parameters are chosen appropriately and κ-noncollapsing holds, subsequences of these rescaled solutions converge (on compact sets) to an orientable ancient κ-solution, yielding a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the contradiction mechanism used to prove Proposition 7.4.1. The argument requires: (i) uniform κ-noncollapsing on bounded scales (Lemma 7.4.2), (ii) curvature bounds at bounded distances from the base point after rescaling (Assertions 1–4), (iii) control that surgeries are pushed away, and (iv) Hamilton compactness plus Shi estimates to obtain smooth limits. The existence of the ancient κ-solution contradicts the assumed minimal violation of the canonical neighborhood assumption.
